paper_design_summary: In a classroom experiment, 305 MBA students in a core strategy course analyzed a business case (Rated), wrote a problem formulation, generated as many strategic options as they wished, and selected the best one. Students were randomized (stratified by section, gender, and consulting background) to no LLM (control), GPT-4 access from the ideation stage onward (partial treatment), or GPT-4 access from the problem formulation stage onward (full treatment). Outcomes are per-participant counts of options and the share coded strategic versus operational by a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo classifier; an appendix follow-up study randomized 24 executive teams (96 executives) to full versus partial LLM timing.

participants.exclusions: Appendix F: 336 students pre-registered, two 'partners' added later, 'bringing the assigned sample to 338. Of these, 305 participated (including the two additions), and 33 were absent' (PDF p. 105, appendix p. 62). Arm-level assignment counts for the 338 are not given; arm counts 103/100/102 are participants. The paper labels its estimates intention-to-treat but analyzes the 305 who participated. Attrition balance in Table F.1 (consulting differs, p = 0.049). Robustness: excluding duration outliers beyond 2 SD leaves 293 (Table A.4); excluding the two additions leaves 303 (Table F.2).
participants.who: MBA students in a core strategy course at a leading business school; mean age 30, 32% female, 31% previously in management consulting; four class sections

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4: standard ChatGPT web interface in sections 1-2; custom wrapper on OpenAI API (gpt-4) pre-loaded with the case in sections 3-4
ai_tool.how_used: Free chat use within the allowed stages. All participants in all conditions received the same optional suggested prompts for problem formulation and ideation (Table A.2). Interaction logs were recorded only for the custom wrapper (88 participants). Option classification used a separate fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo model, not seen by participants.

task.description: Pre-distributed business case (Rated, an unprofitable online reviews platform). Participants (i) articulated the strategic reasons for low profitability (problem formulation), (ii) submitted strategic options one at a time, as many as they wished, and (iii) selected the best option. Done individually in class via an online survey with sequential stage instructions.
task.duration: Mean 44.39 minutes (SD 15.29) for the whole task (PDF p. 14, printed p. 13)

eligibility.reason: S1 randomizes 338 assigned MBA students (305 analyzed: 103 control, 100 partial, 102 full) to GPT-4 access versus no LLM on an idea-generation task (strategic options for a business case). The outcomes are computed on the submitted options: number of options (fluency), categories covered (flexibility), and the strategic share coded by a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 classifier. Criterion 3 rests on fluency and flexibility; the paper has no rated novelty, originality, or creativity, and its headline outcome (strategic focus) is a composition measure coded 'other'. S2 (96 executives, 24 teams, full vs partial AI timing, no no-AI arm) also randomizes AI configuration, but the authors use it for qualitative triangulation.

one_line_finding: LLM access raised the number of options (Partial +2.68, SE 0.55; Full +1.55, SE 0.43; control mean 5.68), but LLM access from problem formulation onward cut the share of strategic options by 0.07 (SE 0.03; control mean 0.57) and the chance of selecting a strategic option by 0.15 (SE 0.07); partial access did not change either (Table 2, PDF p. 38).
open_questions: Design class: the experiment ran in class sessions of a core MBA strategy course on a course case (and in an executive education program for S2). I coded field_rct (coursework); the paper calls it 'laboratory-style' and 'classroom-based', so lab_rct is a defensible alternative.

Is 'strategic options for a business case' a creative or ideation task in scope? I treated it as idea_generation (business ideas). No outcome is a novelty, originality, usefulness, or creativity rating; eligibility rests on fluency and flexibility.

n_randomized: Appendix F gives 338 assigned and 305 participants (33 absent), but arm-level assigned counts are not reported. The text calls the estimates intention-to-treat although absentees are dropped.

Comparison type for problem-stage outcomes (S1-O7, S1-O8): partial had no LLM at the problem-formulation stage, so I coded full vs partial as ai_vs_bau for those; for option-stage outcomes full vs partial is ai_design.

S1-O7 (problem-statement convergence) is scored on the problem formulation, not the ideas; whether it belongs under across_people is a judgment call. Only K-S p-values and a density plot are reported.
notes: Inconsistencies in the document: (1) Interaction-log counts: text (PDF p. 14) and Table A.6 / Figure E.2 say 47 full and 41 partial, but Table A.1 Panel (b) (PDF p. 55) lists Partial 47 and Full 41. (2) Table G.2 labels column (4) 'Difference (3)-(2)' (Partial minus Full), but the printed b values equal Full minus Partial (e.g., 5.08 - 4.58 = 0.50). (3) Section D.2 text says partial treatment p = 0.1 for broad options while Table D.5 marks 0.10** (p < 0.05); the text also cites 'Table D.3' for results that sit in Table D.5. (4) Section 3.2 says coding details are in Appendix A; they are in Appendix C. (5) Section 4 text refers to heterogeneity in 'Appendix E.4'; the heterogeneity analysis is Appendix E.5. Strata FE regressions with robust SEs at the participant (randomization) level for all S1 participant-level outcomes. Mechanism outcomes left out: time spent (Table 4, Table 6 cols. 1, 3), math question accuracy (Table 6 col. 4), overlap measures (Tables E.7, E.8), option-level strategic logit (Table 6 col. 7, N = 1,591 options), share of options matched to LLM output by 15-gram (32.7% full vs 55.6% partial, p = 0.0176, interaction-log subsample of 88), and cosine similarity of problem statements to LLM content (Table E.9, 0.064*** (0.016), N = 88); these are process measures or reliance measures, not creativity of the output. Heterogeneity tables E.10-E.14 and interface split Table A.5 not listed as separate outcomes.
